title: How Long Do Security Camera Recordings Last?
excerpt: Recordings last until storage fills or a plan expires. Learn what sets your retention window and how to export clips before they are overwritten.
body:
Security camera recordings last exactly as long as your storage and settings allow, then they are overwritten, corrupted, or deleted. A motion-only setup on a large card can hold weeks of events; a continuous 4K feed on a small card can fill in hours. There is no single answer, so here is how to calculate yours.

The two questions hiding inside this one

"How long do recordings last" mixes two problems. Retention is how long footage stays viewable before it is overwritten or expires. Lifespan is how long the storage medium itself keeps working. Retention is a math problem you can solve tonight; lifespan is a hardware problem you solve with backups.

Where your footage actually lives

  • SD or microSD cards: cheap, local, and always looping. The camera overwrites the oldest footage when the card fills, and cards fail silently, so assume one will eventually die mid-recording.
  • NVR or DVR systems: hard drives sized in terabytes that overwrite the oldest files on the same principle, but hold weeks or months depending on drive size and resolution.
  • Cloud storage: retention is set by your plan, commonly around thirty days, sometimes far less on free tiers.

The math that sets your retention window

Three variables decide everything: resolution, frame rate, and recording mode. Double the pixel count and you roughly quadruple the storage need, because 4K has four times the pixels of 1080p. Higher frame rates add a smaller but real cost. Recording mode dwarfs both.

Motion-only versus continuous: the biggest lever

Continuous recording writes every second, so a modest card fills fast. Motion-only writes only when pixels change, stretching the same card from days to weeks of real events. The tradeoff: motion-only can miss slow, steady activity that never crosses the detection threshold, like a delivery driver lingering just outside the frame's active area.

What cloud plans keep, and for how long

Most cloud subscriptions hold footage for a fixed window, often about a month, then delete it automatically whether or not anything happened. Free tiers may keep only the most recent clip or a single day. The retention rule lives in the plan settings, not the marketing page, so check there before you assume a recording still exists.

Why free tiers keep so little

Cloud storage costs the provider money every day your clips sit on a server. Free plans are loss leaders, so retention is squeezed to the minimum that still demonstrates the product. Treat free cloud as a trial, not an archive.

What quietly destroys footage

  • Loop overwrite: the default behavior, by design, on any local storage.
  • Power loss mid-write: a corrupted file that no app will play.
  • Plan or account lapse: cloud footage that vanishes on renewal day.
  • Theft of the camera itself: footage stored only on the device goes with it.

Find your real retention number tonight

Open the camera app and look for the storage or playback page. Two numbers matter: how full the storage is right now, and the date of the oldest playable clip. Together they describe your actual retention window better than any specification sheet, because they reflect your resolution, your frame rate, and how busy your scene really is. A quiet hallway and a busy street produce very different windows on identical hardware.

Scroll back until clips stop playing or the timeline goes blank; that boundary is your overwrite horizon. If it sits only a day or two behind today, you are one busy weekend away from losing an event before you notice it. Export anything you might need now, then decide which lever to pull: lower the resolution one step, switch a chatty camera to motion-only, or add storage. Recheck after any settings change, because the window moves every time you touch the math.

How to make recordings last longer

Export event clips the day they happen, to a phone, a computer, or a second cloud account. Check card health in the app monthly and replace any card that throws repeated errors. Reformat the card in the camera itself every few months rather than on a computer, so the file system matches what the camera expects. Turn on cloud backup for flagged events even on local-first cameras. Keep the camera clock synced so exported files line up with real-world times. For a fuller comparison of local versus cloud options, our cloud subscription breakdown and no-subscription camera roundup cover the tradeoffs.
